{"requested_url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sudofx/wake/master/docs/architecture.md", "source_revision": "47e6beda7828527243be52bee76e87cd4e65b51f", "running_revision": "49c9c2bd058c851768320143edc4cf6d6d1e85d4", "source_search": "", "url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sudofx/wake/47e6beda7828527243be52bee76e87cd4e65b51f/docs/architecture.md", "scope": "raw source-controlled WAKE repository text", "excerpt": "# Architecture and limits

See [the reusable kernel contract](kernel.md) for application ownership and the
non-research execution proof, and [installation boundaries](installations.md) for
independent records and runtime lifecycles. These remain inside this repository.

The local [improvement application](improvements.md) uses that same kernel contract
in an explicitly new experiment record. Captured public research informs code
proposals; it does not become writable research authority. Untrusted candidate
code runs only in restricted disposable containers, while the host scores its
outputs. An operator review receipt cannot apply code or grant release authority.

The [autonomous context lane](autonomous-context.md) is a separate WAKE application
policy on the existing per-node native authority. An installed capability permits
one selector-field change, gated by recomputed fixed-task and current-native-state
measurements. Proposal generation, adoption and rollback require no per-change
human review. Metadata events preserve research versions and history; candidate
data cannot replace the evaluator, widen permissions, modify code or create a
competing research store. Native replay owns the policy after restart.

> **Current specification.** This document explains why the present system is shaped this way: its trust boundary, durable record, governance model and known limits. Current local procedures belong in `standalone.md`; public mirror publishing belongs in `cloud.md`. Maintainer navigation, environment checks and reproducible validation guidance belong in `development.md`.

**WAKE✳︎** is infrastructure for continuity of accountable work, not continuity of a model instance. Its stable sequence is **Record → Context → Proposal → Governance → Transition → Receipt**. {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=theoretical+frameworks+distinguishing+between+adaptive+compliance+and+failures+of+epistemic+independence+in+autonomous+systems&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"From Executor to Orchestrator: The Pharmacology Scientist in the Age of Agentic AI.\", \"abstract\": \"Drug development productivity has not improved despite five decades of computational advancement, with the probability that a compound entering Phase I achieving regulatory approval remaining near 10%. Each automation wave increased throughput while leaving the interpretive bottleneck intact; scientists continued to formulate questions, evaluate outputs, and make advancement decisions regardless of how fast data accumulated upstream. Agentic AI systems capable of reasoning, planning, and executing multi-step analyses without continuous human instruction represent the first class of ubiquitous computational tools with the architectural potential to compress this bottleneck, but the implications extend beyond efficiency. As computational systems begin to perform interpretation, execution, and evaluation steps that previously required human judgment, the scientist's contribution shifts from conducting analyses to specifying objectives precise enough for autonomous execution and evaluating recommendations that may be difficult to verify independently. Whether this shift improves aggregate productivity depends on whether autonomous systems address the fundamental causes of clinical failure, including insufficient efficacy, inadequate safety prediction, and poor preclinical translation, rather than merely accelerating the analytical work surrounding them. This review examines what clinical pharmacology scientists must become as these systems enter routine practice. The competencies required for effective orchestration differ from those emphasized in traditional pharmaceutical training, and existing governance structures do not address the failure modes that accompany delegation of scientific judgment to autonomous systems.
